props.title: Intolerance
props.initialSlug: Epic tale of hatred across four time periods

sections.content: Intolerance stands as D.W. Griffith's most ambitious and revolutionary achievement, interweaving four parallel storylines across different historical periods. After facing criticism for The Birth of a Nation (1915), Griffith crafted this epic as both a response and an innovative leap in cinematic storytelling. The film's revolutionary cross-cutting between ancient Babylon, biblical Judea, Renaissance France, and modern America established techniques still studied and emulated today. Its massive sets, particularly the Babylon sequences, set new standards for production design that influenced everything from Ben-Hur (1925) to Cleopatra (1963).

sections.content: The film's technical innovations cannot be overstated. Griffith's "Mountain of Time" editing technique, where he rapidly cuts between parallel stories to build tension, laid groundwork for modern montage theory. The massive crowd scenes, featuring thousands of extras, established a scale of filmmaking that Hollywood would chase for decades. Metropolis (1927) and Ben-Hur (1959) directly borrowed from Griffith's ambitious vision of what cinema could achieve.

The Babylon sequences remain the most influential. Their elaborate sets stood 160 feet high and stretched for blocks, creating a scale of production design unmatched until Cleopatra (1963). Modern epics like Gladiator (2000) and Kingdom of Heaven (2005) still reference Griffith's Babylon in their ancient city designs. The film's famous tracking shots through the festivities influenced Orson Welles' work in Citizen Kane (1941). SUBHEAD: Legacy and Modern Influence

sections.content: Contemporary filmmakers continue drawing from Intolerance's innovative narrative structure. Cloud Atlas (2012) echoes Griffith's interweaving timelines, while Babel (2006) adopts his cross-cultural storytelling approach. Even Christopher Nolan's Dunkirk (2017) uses Griffith's temporal cross-cutting techniques to build tension across different timeframes. The film's ambitious failure - it was a box office disaster that nearly bankrupted Griffith - paradoxically secured its place in cinema history as a testament to uncompromising artistic vision.
